summary: Specifies the procedure for registering RTP payload formats as media types, using audio, video, or other media subtype names. This lets text-based descriptions or control protocols identify what an RTP stream contains. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Audio and video streams need labels so receivers know what is inside the box. This note explains how to officially register a label for a new kind of stream.

questions: how to register an rtp payload format
how does a media type map to sdp
subtitle: How to register an RTP payload format as a media type and map it into SDP.

tldr.problem: A text-based description or control protocol needs a standard way to name the type of an RTP transmission, such as which audio or video format it carries.
tldr.mechanism: RTP payload formats are registered as media types using the general RFC 4288 template, with extra rules for parameters such as rate, channels, ptime and maxptime, and a defined mapping onto SDP lines.
tldr.outcome: The document obsoletes RFC 3555 and removes the registrations that RFC held. The procedure adds no registrations itself. It has since been updated by RFC 8851.

sections.title: Registering RTP Payload Formats
sections.content:
RFC 4288 defines general media type registration procedures that use IANA as a central registry. It covers requirements independent of any particular application environment or transport mode.

RFC 4855 adds the specific requirements for registering media types that identify RTP payload formats, for use with the Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550). The result is useful in a text-based format description or control protocol to identify the type of an RTP transmission.
sections.eli5: There is already a general way to register a label for a kind of file. This note adds the extra rules for labels that describe live audio and video streams.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registration follows RFC 4288 and its template, but some template entries need extra RTP information:

  • Required parameters: if the payload format has no fixed RTP timestamp clock rate, a rate parameter is required.
  • Optional parameters: most audio formats can have channels. Any format may have ptime (recommended milliseconds of media per packet) and maxptime (maximum milliseconds per packet). New parameters MAY be added to an existing RTP type only if they do not change existing functionality and existing implementations can ignore them.
  • Encoding considerations: most RTP payloads are binary or framed data, and this MUST be noted.
  • Published specification: usually an RTP payload format RFC, which MUST include the RTP timestamp clock rate.
  • Restrictions on usage: MUST note that the type is defined for transfer via RTP, particularly if it depends on RTP framing.

Three cases are described: a type not yet registered gets a new registration, an existing non-RTP type has its restrictions changed to allow RTP, and an existing RTP type can be updated to allow non-RTP protocols such as SMTP or HTTP. In each case the parameters must be clearly tied to the mode of transfer they apply to.
sections.eli5: When you register a stream label, you must also say how fast its clock ticks, how many channels it has, and that it travels in RTP.

sections.title: A Sample Registration
sections.content:
The RFC gives a fake media type, audio/example, to show the required text. Its required rate parameter equals the sampling rate, with 8000 as the typical rate. Its optional channels parameter is 1 for mono or 2 for stereo and defaults to 1. Its encoding considerations say it is framed binary data.

Its restrictions on usage say that it depends on RTP framing, so it is only defined for transfer via RTP. References to RFC nnnn stand in for the RFC that would hold the payload format specification.
sections.eli5: The note shows a pretend form for a made-up audio label so you can see what a filled-in form looks like.

sections.title: Sharing a Subtype Name
sections.content:
The same subtype name MUST NOT be shared for RTP and non-RTP (file-based) transfer unless the data format is the same for both. The format counts as the same if the file format is equivalent to a concatenated sequence of payloads from RTP packets, not including the RTP header or any payload-format header. The file MAY have a magic number or other header that RTP does not carry.

The sets of required parameters must also match. Otherwise the formats MUST be registered as separate types, and it is RECOMMENDED that the names be related, such as a common root plus a suffix. For the RTP form, the suffix +rtp is suggested.
sections.eli5: A label may be used for both a file and a live stream only if the contents are really the same. If not, they need two related labels.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP
sections.content:
A media type is written as type "/" subtype *(";" parameter). The Session Description Protocol (RFC 4566), commonly used to describe RTP sessions, takes the pieces as follows:

  • The media type goes in m= as the media name.
  • The subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name.
  • rate and channels also go in a=rtpmap, as clock rate and encoding parameters.
  • ptime and maxptime go in a=ptime and a=maxptime.
  • Format-specific parameters go in a=fmtp. The set is defined by the payload format RFC and MUST NOT be extended by the registration without a revision of that RFC.

Names are case-insensitive: encoding names are commonly shown in upper case, subtype names in lower case, and parameter names are case-insensitive too.
sections.eli5: The label is copied piece by piece onto the call setup sheet, each piece in its own spot, so both ends know what stream is coming.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedure imposes no security considerations on its own, and conforming registrations do not themselves impose risks. Using the registered type can, though. Active content can have malicious side effects, some audio and video encodings are good for hiding data by steganography, and RFC 3550 covers security for RTP transport, including encryption where confidentiality is required.

So each registration MUST state the security considerations that apply. The rest of the section is copied from RFC 4288: an analysis MUST be done for types in the standards tree, and all known risks MUST be identified. A statement of "no security issues" must not be confused with "not assessed". Compression that can expand enormously should be discussed.
sections.eli5: The label itself is harmless, but the stream it names might not be. Every registration has to be honest about possible dangers.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3555
sections.content:
This document updates RFC 3555 to match the revised procedures of RFC 4288. The statement that a type is transferred via RTP moved from encoding considerations to restrictions on usage. It also says when new optional parameters may be added to an existing RTP type, and adds Section 2.2 on sharing names.

The media type registrations that RFC 3555 held for the formats in RFC 3551 were removed. Some were assembled into a companion RFC, RFC 4856, leaving out those registered, or intended to be, in their own payload format RFCs.
sections.eli5: This note replaces an older one. The old list of labels moved to a separate document.

audio/L16; rate=48000; channels=2; ptime=5; emphasis=50-15

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 L16/48000/2
a=fmtp:97 emphasis=50-15
a=ptime:5
